core: Typeface classification as grouping by shared visual features (serifs, stroke contrast, stress/axis)
The broad categories: serif, sans-serif, script, display/decorative, monospace
Serif sub-classes: old style/humanist, transitional, modern/Didone, slab serif, with defining features and example typefaces
Sans-serif sub-classes: grotesque, neo-grotesque, geometric, humanist, with defining features and example typefaces
The rough historical evolution of these categories
How category guides appropriate use (body-text readability, screen vs print, headline/short-text roles, tone)

claims.claim: The broadest division of typefaces is serif versus sans-serif, where a serif is a small stroke attached to the end of a letter's main strokes and sans-serif faces lack them.

Serif typefaces are grouped into four historical sub-classes: old style/humanist (low contrast, diagonal stress, bracketed serifs; e.g., Garamond, Bembo), transitional (more contrast, more vertical stress; e.g., Times New Roman, Baskerville), modern/Didone (extreme contrast, vertical stress, thin unbracketed serifs; e.g., Bodoni, Didot), and slab serif (heavy blocky serifs, low contrast; e.g., Clarendon, Rockwell).

Sans-serif typefaces are grouped into grotesque (early sans-serifs; e.g., Akzidenz-Grotesk, Franklin Gothic), neo-grotesque (mid-20th century, smooth and neutral; e.g., Helvetica, Univers), geometric (built from circles and squares; e.g., Futura), and humanist (calligraphic proportions with stroke variation; e.g., Gill Sans, Frutiger, Verdana, Calibri).

The distinguishing visual features across categories are the presence/shape of serifs, the amount of stroke contrast (thick-thin variation), and the stress or axis (diagonal vs vertical) of rounded letters.

Script faces imitate handwriting/calligraphy (formal and casual), display/decorative faces are designed for large sizes and short text (headlines), and monospace (fixed-width) faces give every character the same horizontal width, descending from the typewriter and used for code and tabular data; scripts and display faces are unsuited to long body text.

The Vox-ATypI classification, devised by Maximilien Vox in 1954 and adopted by ATypI in 1962, organizes Latin type into groups (humanist, garalde, transitional, didone, mechanistic/slab, lineal sans-serifs with grotesque/neo-grotesque/geometric/humanist subgroups, plus calligraphics); ATypI de-adopted it in 2021.

Sans-serif faces became prevalent for on-screen text partly because on lower-resolution displays fine details like serifs could disappear or distort; the blanket claim that serif type is inherently more readable than sans-serif is contextual and not settled by evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether serif type is more readable than sans-serif type.
positions: A common design convention holds serif text is easier to read in long print passages.
Reference sources note sans-serif is often preferred on screens, and readability studies do not conclusively favor one category; results depend on size, medium, and reader.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as convention and context, not settled science: the lesson states the serif-superiority claim is not settled and that sans-serif spread on screens partly because low-resolution displays blurred fine serifs, a constraint that modern high-resolution screens weaken.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Boundaries between sub-classes and terminology (e.g., 'old style' vs 'humanist' vs 'garalde').
positions: Everyday designer usage uses looser labels (serif/sans-serif and four sub-classes each).
Formal systems such as Vox-ATypI split more finely (e.g., humanes vs garaldes) and were themselves de-adopted in 2021.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the practical everyday categories and notes the formal Vox-ATypI system separately, acknowledging categories are human conventions with fuzzy edges.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft (if any) contained only generic placeholder boilerplate about a 'foundational concept'; no substantive classification claims were present, so all of it was discarded and rewritten from sources.

sourceRecords.title: Serif (typeface classification)
sourceRecords.notes: Well-cited encyclopedia article. Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: definition of a serif; the four serif sub-classes (old style/humanist ~1465, low contrast, diagonal stress, bracketed serifs, e.g. Garamond/Bembo; transitional mid-1700s, more contrast, more vertical stress, e.g. Times New Roman/Baskerville; Didone late 1700s, extreme contrast, vertical stress, thin unbracketed serifs, e.g. Bodoni/Didot; slab serif ~1817, heavy serifs as thick as strokes, e.g. Clarendon/Rockwell); and the note that serifs are widely used for print body text while sans-serifs are often considered more legible on screens. Used only to verify facts; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Sans-serif (typeface classification)
sourceRecords.notes: Well-cited encyclopedia article. Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: the four sans-serif sub-classes (grotesque, early 19th-20th c., limited stroke variation, e.g. Akzidenz-Grotesk/Franklin Gothic/News Gothic; neo-grotesque mid-20th c., smooth and neutral, e.g. Helvetica/Univers, tied to the Swiss/International Typographic Style; geometric 1920s, circles and squares, near-circular O and single-story a, e.g. Futura/Erbar/Kabel; humanist, calligraphic proportions and stroke variation, e.g. Gill Sans/Optima/Frutiger/Verdana/Calibri); that sans-serifs became prevalent for on-screen text because at low resolution fine serifs may disappear or distort; and monospace/fixed-width and display context. Facts only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Vox-ATypI classification
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports: the Vox-ATypI system was devised by Maximilien Vox in 1954, adopted by the Association Typographique Internationale (ATypI) in 1962, and became British Standard BS 2961:1967; its groups include classicals (humanist/garalde/transitional), moderns (didone, mechanistic/slab, lineal sans-serifs subdivided into grotesque/neo-grotesque/geometric/humanist), and calligraphics (glyphic/script/graphic/blackletter/gaelic); ATypI de-adopted the system on 27 April 2021 to develop a more inclusive classification. Facts only; no wording reproduced.
